doc.title: John Heard interviewed by Monk Rowe and Michael Woods, Scottsdale, Arizona, March 4, 1995

title: Growing up in Pittsburgh's jazz heritage without formal training
summary: Pittsburgh's many jazz greats formed his education; he had no formal training, and Pittsburgh's corporate offices supported the arts.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: We were talking with Red about the influence of the blues in Chicago, and Pittsburgh — what was happening in Pittsburgh when you were a kid? Was there a certain big thing in the town, or was it like just —

Well you’ve got to realize I grew up with a huge, you know, a huge reservoir of like jazz. The institutions that came out of Pittsburgh, you know, Earl “Fatha” Hines, Mary Lou Williams, Billy Eckstine, Art Blakey, Billy Strayhorn, oh it goes on and on and on, Henry Mancini, Georgie Benson, you know, it just keeps going. So when I grew up, that’s why — Paul Chambers, Ray Brown, Joe Pass, you know, so when you’re playing bass a guy will come up to you and say, “Man you ain’t never gonna be another Ray Brown, why don’t you go home and practice” and you know that kind of stuff. That’s how I grew up. Because I never had any formal education.
No. I just grew up hanging out with all that, you know, heritage from that little town. An unusual little town, you know?
But that in itself is an education, isn’t it?

That was my education. And a lot of Pittsburgers don’t know anything about, you know, math as far as music and technical things. Erroll Garner couldn’t read a note. None of those people could read. So that’s how we grew up. Well Pittsburgh had that thing happening anyway because of all of the corporate home offices. At that time there was the large home offices for private big businesses like Gulf and Westinghouse’s home office was there, U.S. Steel, Jones & Laughlin, you had Rockwell, you had Heinz. You had 54 or 55 corporate offices at that time. And they were you know, kicking back into the town, into the arts. You know that. [I’m talking to Mary.]
